tool.name: MaximumInscribedGeometry

summary.para: Finds the largest circle, rectangle, convex polygon (MCP) or ellipse -- or all four -- that fits entirely inside each polygon, with interior holes acting as barriers: the deliberate dual of Esri's Minimum Bounding Geometry, which fits shapes around features instead. The circle is exact; the rectangle searches every orientation (or one you fix); the convex polygon is the classic potato peeling problem solved on a controllable discretization; the ellipse is always genuinely inside. Every shape carries its geodesic area and dimensions. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
Finds the largest shape of a chosen kind that fits entirely inside each input polygon -- the biggest clearing in a forest gap, the widest circular habitat core, the largest rectangular study plot a corridor can hold, the roomiest convex region among barriers. Interior holes block the shapes, exactly as islands block the Longest Line in Polygon (Fetch) tool; together the two tools form the classic "sticks and potatoes" pair of computational geometry.
The dual of Minimum Bounding Geometry. Esri's tool fits circles, rectangles and hulls around features; this one fits them inside. There is no Esri equivalent at any license level.
Circle. Exact: the center of the maximum inscribed circle always sits on the polygon's medial axis, and the tool finds it there and then refines it against the true boundary. This is the largest circular buffer the polygon can contain -- the polygon's "widest spot".
Rectangle. The tool sweeps every orientation, solves each one exactly on a fine grid, refines the best angles on finer grids, and finally pushes all four sides outward against the true boundary. An optional fixed azimuth (Advanced) constrains the rectangle to one orientation instead -- for survey plots that must run north-south, for example. Reported with its length, width and azimuth.
Convex polygon (MCP). The famous potato peeling problem: the largest convex region inside a polygon. Solving it exactly on the continuous polygon takes on the order of n-to-the-seventh time (Chang and Yap 1986) -- hopeless in practice -- so, in the spirit of Aronov, van Kreveld, Loeffler and Silveira ("Peeling Meshed Potatoes", Algorithmica 60:349-367, 2011, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00453-009-9346-8), the tool solves the problem exactly on a discretization (interior candidate points plus the polygon's own vertices), then polishes the winning vertex chain outward against the true boundary. The result is always truly convex and truly inside; a finer Detail setting can only enlarge it. Convex inputs return the polygon itself, exactly. Think of it as the largest region a Minimum Convex Polygon home range could occupy without touching any barrier.
Ellipse. Uses the conic-linearization method of Hall-Holt, Katz, Kumar, Mitchell and Sityon ("Finding large sticks and potatoes in polygons", SODA 2006, 474-483, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1109557.1109610): boundary sample points are lifted into five dimensions, where every candidate maximum ellipse becomes a facet of a convex hull. The candidates -- plus warm starts from the inscribed circle, the rectangle's ellipse and the convex polygon's inner John ellipse -- are then polished directly against the true boundary edges and shrunk-to-fit, so the reported ellipse is always genuinely inside. For convex inputs the John-ellipse route makes the answer exact.
Outputs. One polygon feature class; with "All four" each input feature gets one row per shape, told apart by the Shape_Kind field. Every row carries the geodesic Area_m2, the center coordinates, and its own measures -- Radius_m (circle), Length_m / Width_m / Azimuth (rectangle), MajAxis_m / MinAxis_m / Azimuth (ellipse), NumVerts (convex polygon) -- plus any transferred attribute fields (reserved names arrive under a Src_ prefix). Measures not applicable to a shape are null (-999 in shapefiles).
Speed and accuracy (Advanced). The Detail distance controls the discretization for all four shapes: the boundary sampling, the rectangle grids and the convex-polygon candidates. Blank picks a sensible automatic value (about 1/150 of each feature's extent). The convex polygon (MCP) is the shape most sensitive to it -- its vertices come from candidate points spaced at this distance, so a smaller Detail can find a genuinely larger polygon -- while the circle, rectangle and ellipse are all refined against the true boundary afterward, so for them Detail mostly trades speed for search thoroughness. The simplify tolerance pre-simplifies each boundary before any fitting, exactly as in the Fetch tool -- invaluable for raster-traced polygons whose stair-step boundaries carry thousands of meaningless vertices; the shapes can shift by roughly the tolerance. Both are in the Units dropdown's units, not the polygon's coordinate-system units. The progress bar reports each polygon and stage as it works.
Geometry notes. Layer selections are honored; multipart features report the best shape over their parts (the Part field says which); true-curve boundaries are densified automatically. Geographic (latitude/longitude) polygons are solved in per-feature azimuthal-equidistant working projections, so radii, lengths and areas are true geodesic meters at any latitude.

dialogReference.para: The polygons to fit shapes inside -- habitat patches, forest gaps, lakes, corridors, management units. Interior holes act as barriers the shapes must avoid. A layer selection is honored.
Circle: the largest inscribed circle (exact -- the polygon's widest spot).
Rectangle: the largest inscribed rectangle, at any orientation or at a fixed azimuth.
Convex polygon (MCP): the largest convex region -- the classic potato-peeling problem.
All four: one row per shape per feature, told apart by Shape_Kind.

param.name: transfer_fields
param.displayname: Attribute fields to transfer to the output

dialogReference.para: Fields whose values ride along onto every output shape, next to the automatic Src_FID. Reserved or conflicting names arrive under a Src_ prefix with the source values intact.

The inscribed shapes as polygons: Src_FID, Part, Shape_Kind, geodesic Area_m2, center coordinates, and each shape's own measures (radius; length, width and azimuth; major and minor axes; vertex count), plus transferred fields.
The working resolution for all four shapes (boundary sampling, rectangle grids and convex-polygon candidates), in the units below. Blank picks about 1/150 of each feature's extent automatically.

Its practical effect differs by shape: the convex polygon (MCP) is the most sensitive, because its vertices come from a grid of candidate points spaced at this distance -- a smaller Detail can find a genuinely larger polygon. The rectangle uses it for the orientation-sweep grids but then grows against the true boundary, and the circle and ellipse are refined against the true boundary regardless -- for those three, Detail mostly trades speed for search thoroughness rather than final precision.

param.name: simplify_tolerance
param.displayname: Simplify tolerance (pre-simplify the boundaries before fitting)

dialogReference.para: Optional: simplify each boundary by this distance (in the units below, not the polygon's coordinate-system units) before any fitting -- the same speed-up as the Fetch tool's tolerance. A raster-traced polygon carries a stair-step vertex at every cell corner; a tolerance near the cell size removes them and speeds every stage, while the shapes can shift by roughly the tolerance. Leave blank to honor the boundary exactly as digitized.

param.name: linear_units
param.displayname: Units for Detail and the simplify tolerance

dialogReference.para: Meters, Kilometers, Feet or Miles. Output measure fields are always in meters.

param.name: fixed_azimuth
param.displayname: Fixed rectangle azimuth (optional -- blank searches all orientations)

dialogReference.para: Optional: constrain the rectangle to one orientation (degrees clockwise from north) instead of searching every angle -- for plots that must run north-south, or align with a management grid. Blank finds the best orientation freely.

scriptExample.title: Maximum Inscribed Geometry example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: All four inscribed shapes for every habitat patch, with a simplify tolerance for raster-traced boundaries.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # geometry_type: "Circle" / "Rectangle" / "Convex polygon (MCP)" / # "Ellipse" / "All four" # linear_units: "Meters" / "Kilometers" / "Feet" / "Miles" arcpy.jenness.MaximumInscribedGeometry( in_features=r"D:\data\habitat.gdb\patches", geometry_type="All four", transfer_fields="Patch_Name", out_features=r"D:\data\habitat.gdb\patches_inscribed", simplify_tolerance=30.0, linear_units="Meters")
